newsitem.title: GERMANY: German call money steady after Buba injects funds.
newsitem.headline: German call money steady after Buba injects funds.

text.p: German call money rates traded steady at three percent on Wednesday even after the Bundesbank surprised markets with a more generous than expected 6.4 billion mark net injection into the system.

While rates traded between 3.05/07 percent early on Tuesday, they had slipped to three percent in late day trading, which prompted several dealers to revise their earlier made forecasts that the Bundesbank would inject funds on Wednesday.
Some dealers said rates may slide below the three percent level later, but the majority predicted the net addition of funds would be needed after all, preventing a sharp slide.

The Bundesbank awarded a repo pact for 83.4 billion marks to replace an expiring 77 billion mark repo pact. While the market had bet on an addition early on Tuesday morning in light of some tightness in the market, the mood appeared to have changed by the afternoon when rates were coming off.

"But the Bundesbank usually calculates these things quite carefully, so I don't think that today's amount of funds will prove to be too much. We will need these funds so that there will be no wild gyrations in rates," a dealer said.
Looking ahead to Thursday, dealers had mixed opinions about what the Bundesbank may or may not announce.
On Thursday the policy-setting council will discuss its next money supply target, which will be announced at a news conference at 1300 GMT.

Dealers said in light of Wednesday's news that November M3 growth slowed to eight percent from 8.4 percent and that the Bank of France nudged its interest rates lower on Tuesday, chances had increased that the bank could cut its repo rate.
The central bank's main money market rate, the repo, has been fixed at three percent since late August and there is a minority view among independent economists that the rate could be eased again.

But many money market dealers said Bundesbank council members had hinted often in recent weeks that there was no need to adjust interest rates at the moment which led them to believe the council would not nudge the repo rate lower now.
Rather they said the Bundesbank may prefer to wait until next year to use any room it may see to ease the money market rate still lower.
Dealers said last-minute holiday shopping sprees, which raise the demand for cash in circulation, could have been one key factor behind the day's generous award.

Banks' daily holdings in accounts at the Bundesbank stood at 40.7 billion marks on Tuesday after 38.6 billion marks on Monday. The monthly average rate also rose to 40.0 billion marks from 39.9 billion marks.
Lombard borrowings were negligible after banks borrowed 100 million marks on Monday.
The Frankfurt Interbank Overnight Average FIONA= was set at 3.02733 percent on Wednesday after 3.06425 percent on Tuesday.
